title: Adding Default Settings to Increase Compliance
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Uses the well-documented success of automatic retirement-plan enrollment (opt-out instead of opt-in) to argue that leaders chasing low compliance on beneficial programs should consider making them the default rather than continuing to push for voluntary adoption. Notes people tend to stick with whatever is set as the default and rarely push back or opt out once enrolled. Offers a long list of organizational processes -- from meeting length to AI meeting notes to charitable giving -- that could benefit from default-setting redesign, with the caveat that defaults must remain transparent, genuinely beneficial to the user, and easy to opt out of.
points: Automatic (opt-out) enrollment in retirement savings plans has more than doubled compliance in many organizations compared to opt-in requirements.
People tend to stick with whatever is set as the default and rarely push back or actively opt out, making default-setting a powerful low-friction lever.
Ethical use of defaults requires transparency, genuine benefit to the user, and an easy, penalty-free opt-out -- otherwise the tactic crosses into manipulation.
quotes: Unless the policy or initiative is viewed negatively, a low compliance rate usually means one thing: It is harder than it should be to comply.

When the initiative, policy, or program is in the favor of team members, make it the default setting. Asking people to opt out of a favorable program as opposed to opt in changes compliance in a big way.

To reduce the friction of having team members fill out paperwork to opt in, many organizations now automatically enroll team members by default while giving them the choice to opt out. This has more than doubled compliance rates for savings plans in many organizations.
The good news is that people tend to stick with default settings or options. They generally don’t push back or opt out.
As long as the defaults are transparent, benefit the user, and allow for easy opt-out with no hidden steps or penalties, leaders should consider adding more.
Well-designed default settings subtly guide behavior, reduce friction, and boost compliance. Making the right choice, the easy choice, turns friction into workflow.
